newsitem.title: UK: British shares leap to record closing high.
newsitem.headline: British shares leap to record closing high.

text.p: Britain's blue chip FTSE 100 stock index leapt to a record closing high on Thursday as Wall Street rose close to all-time peaks, British interest rates were left unchanged and official figures showed a drop in inflation.

The FTSE 100 index closed 38.6 points higher at 4,197.5, surpassing the previous closing peak of 4,168.2 set on January 14 and leaving the index up 141 points or 3.5 percent from the end of last week.
Traders said the UK equity market had gained fresh life this week as fears that rates would rise early in 1997 to tame inflation pressures proved unfounded.
"The market's just incredible," said one trader, "obviously the inflation data helped and the pressure on interest rates has been relieved."

Britain's underlying inflation rate dropped to 3.1 percent in December from 3.3 percent the month before, adding to signs of slack price pressures following mixed reports from retailers that Christmas trading had fallen short of some expectations.
UK government gilts rose sharply on the news, dragging shares up in their wake.
Later the Bank of England indicated no change in the UK's 6.0 interest rate following yesterday's regular policy meeting between Bank governor Eddie George and Chancellor Kenneth Clarke.
George had been expected to push for a rate rise, yet with inflation showing no immediate signs of resurfacing, Clarke was able to resist any Bank pressure.

And with shares continuing to rise across continental Europe, the British market was able to make further progress. By early afternoon the FTSE 100 reached an intraday record of 4,198.9, its third this week.

Strategists said a dip in the inflation figures justified the decision to keep interest rates on hold for the time being, but rates may still have to rise in February if Clark is to meet his 2.5 percent target for underlying inflation.

Dealers pointed out that the stock market had so far followed its traditional pattern of rising in January, when seasonal inflows of cash into investment funds produce what is regularly one of the market's strongest months of the year.
Assuming no sell-off on Wall Street, market watchers said the New Year bull run in UK stocks could run for some time yet.
But they warned that fears of a rise in interest rates -- and jitters of an election that must be held by May -- could resurface to spoil the party at any stage.
"For the time being shares are only reacting to good news and we have got a raging bull market," said the head of equity trading at one top broking house.
"But sooner or later it will settle down and people will realise that rates could still go up. In some ways it would have been better to get the rise over this week."
